1	# Task 11: Floating islands in a sunset sky
2	
3	Build a single-page browser app with the provided framework, served by vite. It must render one full-viewport canvas with id #app. The scene is a sky full of floating rock islands at sunset. Show at least 6 islands of different sizes, each a chunky rock underside tapering downward (cone or inverted-lump shapes) topped with a grassy surface and a few simple trees or crystals. Islands bob gently up and down at different speeds and phases. A warm orange to pink gradient sky fills the background with a large low sun, and 8 or more soft cloud banks drift slowly past at different depths. A thin waterfall or particle stream falls from the largest island. Distance haze makes far islands paler and bluer. The camera slowly drifts in a wide arc, looping every 40 to 60 seconds, with no user input. Do not rely on external downloads; build everything procedurally. Keep it above 30 fps on a mid-range laptop.

content.thinking:
I'm thinking through sky rendering reliability in headless WebGL, planning to use a gradient sky with horizon glow and sun disc, and considering whether to add an actual emissive sphere positioned low on the horizon as a real sun object rather than a faked glow.

Fog could wash out a distant sun sphere, so I'm weighing whether to disable fog on that material versus controlling haze directly through island material colors. Since materials seem static and can't be updated per frame as the camera moves, real fog via effects.fog is probably safer for distance haze, while giving the sun sphere its own unlit material with fog disabled — I want to check the water custom shader recipe for the right material format.

I'm checking whether material transparency and fog settings affect the background, then sketching a simplified sky setup using a gradient with zenith, horizon, ground colors and a low-elevation sun disc to reduce unknowns.

For positioning, I need the sun azimuth to align with the camera's general viewing direction (toward -z), and since the camera arcs about ±30° around that direction, the sun at azimuth 0 will drift across the frame but stay mostly visible if I keep the swing to roughly ±28°. I'll make the camera's path a smooth sine-based loop over about 50 seconds so it closes naturally, with a bit of height variation added for interest.

I'm weighing whether to add a separate sun sphere for visual robustness, but worry about perspective misalignment since the sky's sun disc is effectively at infinite distance while a sphere would be at a finite distance and shift noticeably as the camera moves — so I'd need to reposition it every frame relative to the camera to keep it aligned. That raises the question of how to actually drive the camera each frame: whether there's a setPose-style API with a "cut" option to avoid smoothing lag, and whether the camera controller is guaranteed to be defined by default or if I need a fallback approach.

content.thinking: Since the camera system is on by default, I'm thinking of using setPose with cut:true in onFrame to set a static camera pose each frame, bypassing damping, with no fallback needed if that's undefined. Let me check CameraController.setPose to confirm this behavior.

I'm checking whether the controller stays active once pose overrides are applied each frame, since isActive depends on the last pose delta being nonzero—so I need to confirm the idle check doesn't fire prematurely before the override's delta registers on the next update cycle.

I'm also weighing whether to use the rail rig with looped points instead of setPose, since a rail rig might handle continuous motion more naturally, but I'm unsure if camera updates even run every frame or only when the frame loop decides to re-arm—so I need to trace where camera.update actually gets called relative to the rendering loop.

Since setPose re-arms the tick each call, the order matters: the camera tick (registered earlier) runs first each frame using the previous overrides, then my callback sets new ones, creating a one-frame lag. This means the sun sphere's position, computed in the same frame as my override, will be slightly mismatched with the camera's delayed update, but that's an acceptable tradeoff.

I'm weighing whether to keep the sun sphere alongside the sky disc, since the sky disc exists at infinity and isn't affected by camera translation. I'll keep both but align the sphere precisely along the sky sun's direction at a large distance so the discs coincide, sizing it to roughly a 5.3° angular radius so it reads as a large, visible sun in screenshots, and giving it a simple gradient shader for glow.

Writing shader code for the halo...

Vertex precision should be fine since the sphere's scaling happens through the model matrix. Now I'm planning the cloud banks—building 12 drifting clusters of flattened spheres per bank, each wrapping across the X axis, with soft pbr materials tinted pink/white and emissive to catch the sunset glow.

content.thinking:
I'm using unlit, fog-disabled materials for the sun — a solid disc plus a larger, semi-transparent halo sphere with alpha blending, though I'm a little wary that the blend mode might not render as expected.

For clouds I'm leaning toward lit, opaque lump-spheres with emissive warmth and fog-driven haze rather than transparency, since overlapping transparent shapes would create visible seams. For lighting, I'm reconsidering the sun direction so the islands aren't backlit and silhouetted from camera view.

I'm planning a rim-lit key directional from the sun's position shifted slightly ahead-right, paired with a warm hemisphere light for sky/ground fill and a secondary pinkish fill directional from the camera side to soften shadowed faces, skipping shadow casting to save cost. I'm weighing whether to layer in a golden-hour look preset for grading and bloom, but worried it might override my custom sky setup, so I'm leaning toward building the lighting manually instead.

Writing scene background config...

Using exp2 fog mode so it stays applied just to depth-faded elements, keeping the sun and sky largely unaffected while clouds get hazed naturally. Now I'm working out the world layout: placing islands across a wide x-range and varying depth, with the camera orbiting a center point and sweeping a modest arc angle over time for a slow panning effect.

I'm checking that the camera's swept path stays far enough from the near islands so nothing clips through the view, while still allowing a dramatic island to sit fairly close for visual impact.

I'm also calculating the horizontal field of view at the main target distance so I know how wide to spread the islands across x, then sketching out the island layout starting with a large main island with a waterfall edge and some grassy lumps on top.

For the underside, I'm flipping a cone shape to point downward for the rocky base, using faceted geometry with low radial segments for a chunky rock look, plus asymmetric lumps and smaller hanging rocks for detail.

I'm uncertain whether the cone's base diameter scales as size or 2×size given the default unit radius of 1, so I want to pick a scale factor that avoids ambiguity in the crown proportions.

Switching to using cylinders with explicit radiusTop/radiusBottom instead of cones for cleaner control — a tapered cylinder with radiusTop 0 gives me a pointed shape without the cone's scaling ambiguity, and I'm using a small nonzero radiusBottom to avoid degenerate normals at the tip. For crystals, I'm considering a hexagonal prism built from a low-segment cylinder with tapered ends to mimic a faceted gem shape.

For performance, I'm thinking through whether instanced meshes nested inside a group will inherit the group's transform for the bobbing animation — since that's uncertain, I'll stick with plain individual primitives inside groups and just keep per-island object counts modest to stay within draw call budgets.

Estimating total draws: roughly 160 for island trees/rocks/grass plus 56-70 for cloud banks plus waterfall geometry, landing around 250-300 draw calls total, which should run fine even under SwiftShader at low resolution. I'll sketch out the island generator function next, applying size and scale manually within each constructor.

Defining island layers...

Still defining rock and lump geometry...

Now I'm adding hills as flattened grass spheres for variation, and setting up the tree structure with trunk cylinders and crown shapes.

For trees, I'll alternate between stacked pine-style crowns and rounded crown spheres, varying colors between greens with warm tints, and scaling tree size based on island radius with randomized placement using polar coordinates biased toward the center.

For crystals, I'm placing clusters of 2-4 tilted hex prisms with pink/cyan emissive glow at scattered points. For the waterfall, I'm adding a thin translucent light-blue stream flowing from the main island's visible front rim down about 60 units, accompanied by roughly 40 small falling droplet spheres sharing coordinated downward motion.

Since the island bobs up and down, I need the waterfall to track that movement — I'm deciding whether to nest the droplets and stream as children of the island group so they inherit local position, or instead keep them in world space and manually update their origin each frame based on the island's computed bob offset, which feels safer given uncertainty about how setPosition behaves on nested children.
